interrogator_dossier:
# Axalta Coating Systems (AXTA) — Event Forensics Dossier
### Prepared 27 July 2026 · Event: all-share merger of equals with AkzoNobel

**The single most important finding first.** The event is real, signed, and progressing — but the payoff our watch board recorded is wrong. Our board carries a target of $42.64 against a live price of $32.34, implying a spread of roughly 32% and a reward-to-risk of 2.48. That target is the naive arithmetic of the exchange ratio times AkzoNobel's share price, and it ignores the single largest term in the deal: AkzoNobel will pay its own shareholders a €2.5 billion special cash dividend *before* completion, and Axalta holders receive none of it. Once that leakage is netted out — exactly as the companies themselves do it in the merger prospectus — the deal is worth about **$33.90** per Axalta share today, not $42.64. Against a live price of $32.76 (last close, 24 July 2026) that is a gross spread of about **3.5%**, not 32%. The asymmetry is not 2.48 to 1 in our favour; it is roughly 0.25 to 1 against us.

---

## 1. The event: what it is, precisely

On 18 November 2025 AkzoNobel (the Dutch paints group, listed in Amsterdam) and Axalta signed a definitive agreement to combine in an all-share merger of equals. Terms:

| Term | Detail |
|---|---|
| Consideration | 0.6539 AkzoNobel ordinary shares per Axalta share. No cash alternative, no collar (a collar is a band that adjusts the ratio if the buyer's stock moves). |
| Ownership split | AkzoNobel holders 55%, Axalta holders 45% of the combined company. |
| Pre-completion distribution | AkzoNobel pays its own shareholders €2.5 billion in cash, less any regular 2026 dividends already paid, immediately before closing. Axalta holders are excluded. |
| Surviving entity | AkzoNobel. Dual-listed on Euronext Amsterdam and the New York Stock Exchange at first, moving to New York only after a transition period. |
| Stated synergies | About $600 million of pre-tax annual cost savings, roughly 90% achieved within three years. |
| Combined scale | About $17 billion of pro-forma 2024 revenue, about $25 billion enterprise value (the equity plus net debt). |
| Company-guided close | "Late 2026 to early 2027." |
| Contractual end date | 18 May 2027, extendable to 18 November 2027. |

Note the last two rows carefully. Our board records a hard date of 31 December 2026. **No such date exists in the contract.** "Late 2026 to early 2027" is management guidance; the only binding deadline is 18 May 2027, and either side can push it to 18 November 2027. A soft guidance window is not a forcing date, and treating it as one overstates how quickly this resolves.

## 2. Is the catalyst real, dated, and binding?

Real and binding: yes, unambiguously. This is a signed merger agreement, not a rumour or a strategic review. The evidence chain is dated and verifiable:

- **18 November 2025** — definitive agreement signed and jointly announced.
- **21 January 2026** — both companies filed their US antitrust notifications under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act (the pre-merger clearance regime).
- **26 January 2026** — pre-notification discussions opened with the European Commission.
- **20 February 2026** — the US Federal Trade Commission issued a "second request," meaning it wants a deep review rather than a quick clearance.
- **13 March 2026** — pre-notification discussions opened with the UK Competition and Markets Authority.
- **3 June 2026** — Nippon Paint and Sherwin-Williams, both of which had approached AkzoNobel, withdrew. AkzoNobel's boards reaffirmed the Axalta merger.
- **23 June 2026** — the US Securities and Exchange Commission declared AkzoNobel's registration statement effective, which is what unlocks the shareholder vote.
- **24 June 2026** — Axalta called its special meeting for 5 August 2026; AkzoNobel called its own meeting for the same day.
- **23 July 2026** — the two companies amended the merger agreement a second time, softening the post-close governance lock-ups after shareholder pushback.

Dated: partially. There is one genuinely hard date nine days out — the **5 August 2026 shareholder votes**. But that is a gating condition, not the value-realising event, and it is widely expected to pass. The value-realising event is regulatory clearance in roughly 30 jurisdictions, and that has no date at all.

## 3. Where the payoff actually sits — the arithmetic

This is the part our board got wrong, so it is worth showing the work. The companies publish their own implied-value calculation in the merger prospectus, and it deducts the pre-completion distribution:

| Reference date | AkzoNobel close | Euro/dollar | Implied value per Axalta share |
|---|---|---|---|
| 17 November 2025 (day before announcement) | €56.64 | 1.159 | ~$30.25 |
| 23 June 2026 (prospectus date) | €59.94 | 1.138 | ~$34.36 |

Back-solving the 23 June figure gives a distribution deduction of about €13.76 per AkzoNobel share — roughly 23% of AkzoNobel's market price. Applying the same method to today: AkzoNobel at €59.26 (27 July 2026), less €13.76, times 0.6539, times a euro/dollar rate of 1.1384, gives **$33.87 per Axalta share**.

Axalta last closed at **$32.76** on 24 July 2026, up 3.4% that session. So:

- Gross spread to the deal's own value: **+3.5%**
- Drop to the undisturbed pre-announcement price of $28.17 (17 November 2025): **−14.0%**
- Reward-to-risk: **about 0.25 to 1**
- Completion probability the market is implying: (32.76 − 28.18) ÷ (33.87 − 28.18) = **about 80%**

An 80% implied completion probability against a 3.5% spread over a five-to-sixteen-month wait is an ordinary, fully-functioning merger-arbitrage price. There is no mispricing here to harvest. The market has done this arithmetic; our board did not.

One further structural point that removes the "fixed payout" comfort entirely: because the consideration is shares with no collar and no cash, **there is no ceiling and no guaranteed number**. An Axalta holder is, in economic substance, long 0.6539 AkzoNobel shares with a 3.5% carry attached. If AkzoNobel falls 15%, so does the Axalta payoff. There is also unhedged currency risk, since the consideration is a euro-denominated security.

## 4. How credible are the sponsors on hitting the date?

High on intent and execution, moderate on timing.

**Green flags.** Both boards unanimously recommend the deal and have reaffirmed it repeatedly. There is no financing condition — this is stock, not a leveraged buyout, so no lender can walk. AkzoNobel has nonetheless pre-funded the special distribution with €600 million and €750 million of new senior notes plus a €1.5 billion revolving facility, which means the cash condition is already solved rather than aspirational. Cevian Capital, an activist holding roughly 5% of AkzoNobel, supports the combination. Competing suitors for AkzoNobel withdrew in June, removing the risk that AkzoNobel's board gets distracted or diverted. And the registration statement went effective on schedule, which is a genuine, checkable milestone rather than a promise.

**Red flags.**
- **The antitrust overlap is the real one.** AkzoNobel and Axalta are both top-tier players in vehicle refinish — the paint sold to collision-repair body shops. This is a concentrated global market, and it is precisely the kind of horizontal overlap that draws remedies. The US Federal Trade Commission's second request, issued 20 February 2026, confirms this is not a formality. Management's own language is telling: they concede "there are areas where at some point we may be discussing remedies," which "can be behavioural remedies… or selective divestments." Filings are pending in roughly 30 countries; any one of them can slow the clock.
- **Timing has already been quietly stretched.** A merger Q&A earlier in 2026 described a "mid-July 2026" shareholder vote and a "year-end 2026" close. The vote landed on 5 August, and the guided close is now "late 2026 to early 2027." That is a modest slip, not a collapse, but it points in the wrong direction.
- **Axalta shareholders are not being paid a premium, and some of them have noticed.** The consideration on the day before announcement was about $30.25 against an undisturbed price of $28.17 — roughly a 7% premium, which is negligible for a change of control. Artisan Partners Global Value (about 0.7% of Axalta) publicly urged holders to reject the deal. Shapiro Capital Management (about 1.1%, a top-25 holder) said it was "very disappointed" and would vote against unless terms improved or alternatives were explored. The 23 July governance amendment — annual director re-election after three years instead of five, and a two-thirds rather than three-quarters board threshold for senior appointments — is a concession, but it is governance, not price. No shareholder who objects to being paid nothing for control has been given anything for control.
- **The vote threshold has a trap door.** Axalta's approval requires a simple majority of votes cast *only if* an accompanying bye-law amendment passes. If that amendment fails, the merger needs a **three-quarters** majority. With two vocal opponents already on the record, that is a low-probability but genuinely fatal branch, and it resolves in nine days.

## 5. The verified downside floor — what actually backstops the price

There is no contractual floor. This is a stock-for-stock merger; there is no cash backstop, no minimum value, and no termination payment flowing to shareholders. The floor is a valuation floor, and it has to be built from the standalone business.

**Anchor one — the undisturbed price.** Axalta closed at **$28.17** on 17 November 2025, the last trading day before the deal was public. On this year's guidance that is about 7.4 times enterprise value to adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EV/EBITDA — the company's value including debt, divided by its cash operating profit). This is the number our board carries as the floor, and it is a defensible one.

**Anchor two — the standalone parts.** Axalta reports two segments. In 2025, Performance Coatings (refinish plus industrial) did $3.28 billion of revenue and Mobility Coatings (light-vehicle and commercial-vehicle original equipment) did $1.84 billion. I estimate segment cash operating profit of roughly $0.83 billion and $0.28 billion respectively, consistent with the $1.11 billion company total. Valuing Performance at 9 times and Mobility at 5 times gives an enterprise value of about $8.9 billion; less net debt of $2.54 billion at 31 March 2026, that is about **$29.60 per share** on 214.0 million shares. A mid-case at 9.5 and 5.5 times gives about $32.20; a generous case at 10.5 and 6 times gives about $36.70.

The two anchors agree: a break sends the stock to something in the **high-$20s**, call it $28. In practice it would likely trade slightly below that on the first day as merger-arbitrage funds unwind in a hurry, then recover toward standalone fair value. So the floor is real but soft — a valuation level that depends on the coatings cycle holding, not a contractual payment that arrives regardless.

**What supports it.** The underlying business is sound and cash-generative. Management guides 2026 to $1.14–1.17 billion of adjusted cash operating profit, adjusted earnings per share of $2.55–2.70, and free cash flow above $500 million. Liquidity at the end of the first quarter was $608 million of cash plus $770 million of undrawn revolver, and the company prepaid $50 million of term loans. Net debt of $2.54 billion is about 2.2 times cash operating profit — comfortable. There is no going-concern issue, no equity issuance programme, no covenant stress, and no financing contingency. On the standard forensic red-flag checklist for event names, Axalta is clean.

**What erodes it.** Guidance is drifting toward the low end on softer demand, and the refinish franchise has a slow structural headwind: collision-avoidance technology reduces accident frequency, which reduces the volume of paint body shops buy. That is a decade-long drag, not a cliff, and it is partly offset by a growing vehicle fleet and more expensive repairs per claim.

## 6. Governance and process integrity

Nothing here suggests a manipulated process, but the shape of the deal deserves naming plainly. A "merger of equals" with no premium, where the larger party pays itself €2.5 billion in cash on the way out and the smaller party receives shares only, is a structure that transfers value toward the acquirer's register. Axalta's holders end up owning 45% of the combined company and 45% of the $600 million of synergies — which, capitalised, is worth roughly $10 per Axalta share if delivered — but they surrendered control to get it, and control normally carries a price. The objecting shareholders are making a coherent argument, not a nuisance one. That said, at 1.8% of the register between them, they lack the votes to block on a simple-majority test.

## 7. What the market is not arguing about

There is no meaningful disagreement left to exploit. The deal has been public for eight months, the terms are fixed and published, the prospectus is effective, both meeting dates are set, the objectors have said their piece in public, and the price sits within a few percent of the terms. This is the opposite of a mispriced special situation: it is a crowded, well-understood arbitrage where the residual return is compensation for regulatory tail risk and for tying up capital, and where our book — which cannot short AkzoNobel to lock the ratio — would be taking the euro-equity risk without the hedge that makes the trade work for professional arbitrageurs.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

The event is credible and on track; the recorded opportunity is not. Everything that can be verified about the merger points to a well-run, well-supported, likely-to-complete transaction — and precisely because it is all of those things, the market has already paid for it. The board's 32% spread is an artifact of omitting the €2.5 billion pre-completion distribution from the target price. Corrected, the spread is 3.5% against a 14% drop to the undisturbed price, with the real deadline fifteen months away rather than five months, and with the payoff floating on a foreign share price we would not be hedging.

The one thing to weigh before sizing anything: **this is not a defined-risk special situation, it is an unhedged long position in AkzoNobel with a small carry.** If the investment case is "we want to own 45% of the world's number-two coatings company as it takes out $600 million of costs," that is a legitimate three-year proposition and should be argued on its merits, at a size and in a book appropriate to a cyclical industrial compounder. It should not be dressed as event arbitrage, because as event arbitrage the numbers do not work.

On the underlying franchise: refinish is a genuinely sticky business — body shops are locked in by colour-matching systems, equipment, and technician training, and they do not switch casually. That is a narrow but real competitive advantage, and it is stable rather than widening or collapsing. Mobility Coatings is far more commoditised and cyclical. The structural threat from safer vehicles is real but slow and manageable, not terminal. The cheapness on display, such as it is, is neither a fear-print nor a value trap — it is simply a fair price for a decent, cyclical, mid-quality industrial.
